title: Neuroscientist 'lost his fear of dying' after near-death experience
excerpt: Neuroscientist Dr Christof Koch says his near-death experience during the Covid-19 pandemic - in which he felt terror and ecstasy and saw an icy blue light - has changed his attitude to death
content:
'I lost fear of dying’ after seeing overwhelming brightness in near-death experience'

Neuroscientist Dr Christof Koch says his near-death experience during the Covid-19 pandemic - in which he felt terror and ecstasy and saw an icy blue light - has changed his attitude to death

14:49, 19 Sep 2026

Stories of near-death experiences stretch back almost to the dawn of time. They can include both the enlightening and the terrifying, and they often change how people face up to death when they come back around.

‌

Neuroscientist Dr Christof Koch appears to have experienced a mixture of both, as he described his "utterly remarkable" experience where he saw "overwhelming brightness" along with "terror and ecstasy" when he had a medical emergency during the Covid-19 pandemic.

‌

He has conducted extensive research into what he terms "power outages" in the brain, motivated partly by his own encounter when he endured what he describes as "a medical emergency" during the initial days of the pandemic.

‌

He recounted the "utterly remarkable" experience to The Times, stating: "I saw overwhelming brightness and felt terror and ecstasy. Nothing else no body, no self, no identity whatsoever. But also no world and no passage of time. Nothing except for an icy blue light."

Dr Koch, who works at the Allen Institute in Seattle, says that the encounter has entirely transformed his perspective on death. Like many individuals who have undergone this phenomenon, he no longer dreads dying: "In people who have undergone a near-death experience this is not uncommon. It's a so-far unexplained benefit."

Discussing the near-death experience [NDE] phenomenon in Scientific American, Dr Koch reveals that approximately one in 10 patients who experience cardiac arrest and are subsequently resuscitated report having an NDE: "Thousands of survivors of these harrowing touch-and-go situations tell of leaving their damaged bodies behind and encountering a realm beyond everyday existence, unconstrained by the usual boundaries of space and time.

"These powerful, mystical experiences can lead to permanent transformation of their lives."

He notes that numerous NDE experiencers describe encountering departed family members or spiritual entities like angels. He outlines how many individuals who've undergone a near-death experience witness their life "flash before their eyes.."

‌

Certain aspects of these accounts can be attributed to basic physiological alterations, he explains. For instance, the "tunnel vision" reported by those who've approached death might result from diminished blood circulation to the eyes.

Nevertheless, other elements of this phenomenon resist straightforward scientific interpretation. In 2006, French anaesthetist and researcher Dr. Jean-Jacques Charbonier presented a compelling case at the First International Conference on Near-Death Experiences.

Article continues below

During major surgery, a female patient suffered cardiac arrest and experienced a near-death episode. Following resuscitation, she remembered feeling as though she had drifted upwards to the operating theatre ceiling.

Floating above the operating theatre ceiling, she claimed she could peer over a partition into the adjacent room. There, she alleged, she witnessed surgeons removing another patient's leg and disposing of the severed limb in a yellow medical waste bag.

Subsequent enquiries, Dr Charbonier stated, confirmed the woman's account was entirely accurate: "People who were brain-dead could see what was going on in a waiting room, or around them, in precise detail. We are not talking about an hallucination here because it was quite real," he said.
